blocks.text: Linda Hanna, Practice Manager

Linda Hanna has joined Meridian as our Practice Manager, and we are glad to have her. The practice has reached the size where engagement paperwork, billing and the tracking of client files need one person who owns them. Linda is that person. In her first days she has already shown us a habit we value in this office: she gives the reason for a request before she makes it.

Linda sits in Operations and reports to Robert Lawrence, Managing Actuary. Her work touches every engagement, though she will not do the actuarial work on any of them. She will prepare and track engagement letters, issue invoices and follow up on the ones that go unpaid, and keep the record of which client data files have arrived and which are still outstanding. She also keeps the calendar of report deadlines. Our deadlines depend on client data, and client data often arrive late or incomplete. When a due date and a data delivery stop lining up, she will often see it before the actuary on the engagement does. We want her to raise it early, and we want the consulting staff to treat that as help.
Her first period is about learning how an assignment moves from a signed letter to an issued report and a paid invoice. We have agreed on the following for her first two months:

items: 1. Read every open engagement letter and the data request that went with it, so she knows what we committed to and what we asked each client to send.
2. Prepare one month-end billing cycle alongside Robert Lawrence, and take over the invoice log from the cycle after that.
3. Set up a single tracking sheet for client data: what was requested, what has arrived and when, and what is still outstanding.
4. Meet each member of the consulting group, one at a time, to learn how each of them wants to hear about late or incomplete data.
5. Look over where signed letters, invoices and client correspondence are filed, and tell us where the filing does not hold together.

blocks.text: Linda is not expected to know actuarial terms on arrival, and nobody here should make her feel she ought to. When a question about a file or an invoice turns on an actuarial point, the actuary on that engagement answers it. Robert Lawrence will sit down with her at the end of each week for those two months to go through what is open. After that, the billing and data records are hers to run.
New associate in the consulting group

Michelle Banks joined us this month as an Actuarial Associate. We have wanted another associate on the valuation side for a while, and we are pleased that it is her. She is starting at an odd time. The whole firm is working from home for now, so her first weeks will run on phone calls, video calls and the shared drive. That is harder on a new person than on the rest of us, and we will check in with her more often than we would across a desk.

Michelle reports to Jennifer Vasquez, Consulting Actuary, and sits with the consulting group. Most of her work will be data validation and benefit calculations. In practice that means testing each census file against the prior year, following up on members who appear, drop out or change status without explanation, and calculating individual benefits under the plan's terms. In time she will also answer questions from fund administrators about how a plan provision works. Administrators act on what we tell them. Each answer has to be correct and has to say what it rests on, including any provision we have read one way when another reading is possible.
None of us can pass on our habits by working beside her, so we have written down what her first period should cover. The items are in rough order:

items: 1. Confirm that her laptop and remote connection work, and that she can open the shared client folders and the valuation files she will be checking.
2. Read the firm's standard wording on data reliance and on the qualifications we attach to results, before she drafts anything a client will see.
3. Work through the census checks on a valuation already under way, with Jennifer Vasquez reviewing each check she makes.
4. Keep her open questions in one numbered list, so that answers by email or on a call can refer back to each item.
5. Hold a standing call with Jennifer Vasquez twice a week through the summer, and move it to weekly when they both agree it is time.

blocks.text: Robert Lawrence will join one of those calls each month to hear how the arrangement is working. We would like to know what is hard to learn at a distance, so that we can make it easier for her and for whoever starts this way next. Her desk will be ready for her when the office opens again.
Good morning Michelle,

Your building access card is ready. The building office has set it up for the lobby turnstiles and for the door to our suite, and the security desk in the lobby will hand it to you on your first morning in, once they have seen photo identification. You do not need to arrange anything with them beforehand.

One point worth knowing: as I understand it, the building now switches off cards that go unused for an extended period. If yours stops working after a stretch at home, the same desk can reactivate it, and there is no need to request a replacement through us.

Karen Harris, consulting group

Karen Harris has joined the consulting group as an Actuarial Associate. We are pleased to have her. Her work will be assumption analysis and the supporting tables for our experience studies, and she brings to it a good eye for a spreadsheet that does not tie out. We have kept her first weeks clear of client deadlines, so that she can learn how we build a study before she is asked to deliver part of one.
Where she fits

Karen reports to Jennifer Vasquez, Consulting Actuary. An experience study has three parts, and we keep them apart. The data show what happened to the members or policies over the study period. The assumptions say what we expected to happen. The actuary then judges how far the first should move the second. Karen will build much of the first part: the exposure and decrement tables, the comparisons of actual to expected, and the exhibits that set them out. She will also be asked to say where the data stop. Some questions go further than a study's data can support, and when they do we want her to say so in plain words. Studies that take in the past couple of years need a further decision about how much weight to give the pandemic experience. That decision is a judgment, and the report will label it as one.
The first weeks
Several of us are back in the office part of the week, so some of this can happen in person. We have set out her first weeks so that each step builds on the one before:

items: 1. Collect her building access card and laptop, and confirm she can reach the shared client folders and the study workpapers.
2. Read the firm's standard language on data reliance and on the qualifications we place on a result.
3. Read the workpapers of a completed experience study, from the data request through to the final exhibits.
4. Rebuild one actual-to-expected table from the raw data and reconcile it to the issued exhibit, noting every difference however small.
5. Meet weekly with Jennifer Vasquez for her first three months to go over her work and what comes next.

blocks.text: One expectation applies from the first day. When a result surprises her, we want to hear about it before anyone explains it. Robert Lawrence reads every experience study before it is issued, and he will want her view of the assumptions when her first study reaches him.
About Meridian Actuarial Advisors

Meridian Actuarial Advisors is a consulting actuarial practice. Our clients are the boards, trustees and officers who answer for long-term obligations: pensions owed to public employees and to the members of multiemployer funds, and the reserves a life insurer holds for the policies it has written. We tell them what those obligations are likely to cost, how much of that estimate rests on assumptions, and what would change it. The decisions are theirs. Our part is to make sure each decision is taken with a clear view of the measurement behind it.
We revise this overview as the practice changes. This version describes the work we take on, the way we handle it, and some of the clients we have served.
The work we take on
Most of our assignments fall into a handful of kinds. Each one starts from the same question: what does the client need to know, and by when?

items: 1. Funding valuations for public retirement systems, with the contribution recommendations their boards act on and the accounting disclosures their auditors require.
2. Experience studies, which compare what actually happened to a plan's members or an insurer's policies with what was assumed, and recommend changes where the data support them.
3. Actuarial services for multiemployer funds: valuations for the trustees, the annual certification of funded status, and the projections behind a funding improvement or rehabilitation plan.
4. Reserve and cash-flow testing work for life insurers, including support for the appointed actuary's opinion.
5. Benefit calculations for fund administrators, and answers to their questions about how a plan provision applies to a particular member.
6. Independent reviews of another actuary's valuation or assumptions, prepared for a board or its counsel.

blocks.text: How we set out a result

Every report we issue states its scope, the data we relied on, and the standards the work was performed under before it says anything about results. After that we keep three things apart. What the data show comes first. What we assumed comes next, with the reason for each assumption. What we conclude comes last, and a conclusion that depends on an assumption gets a paragraph of its own. A board's counsel should be able to read any one of those parts and know which kind of statement it is.

We review data before we rely on them, and we tell the client in writing about anything we could not reconcile. A second actuary reviews every opinion before it leaves the firm. When the professional standards change, we explain the change to clients before it reaches their reports. The revised standard on pension measurement is the present case. It takes effect next year, and from then on our pension funding reports will include a low-default-risk obligation measure, with a short explanation of what that figure measures and how a board might use it.

The people

Robert Lawrence, Managing Actuary, leads the practice and signs its actuarial opinions. Our consulting actuaries scope each assignment and review it before it is issued. Associates and analysts build and maintain the valuation models, check the data, and prepare the exhibits. Our practice manager keeps engagement letters, data requests, deadlines and billing in order, and is often the first to notice when a data delivery and a report date have drifted apart. The consulting group has grown with the work, and each person who joins it learns the same habits of documentation in the first week.
Starting an assignment

A first conversation is usually about the question the client needs answered, and only later about method or fee. If we are not the right firm for that question, we say so then. When we are, the client receives a written proposal, and after it an engagement letter that fixes the scope and the standards before any data are requested. Robert Lawrence is glad to have that first conversation, and enquiries can go to him directly.
Nicole Hanna starts on the valuation team

Nicole Hanna has joined us as an Actuarial Associate, and her first days have gone smoothly. We are glad to have her. She will support the valuation team, which is where much of the firm's year is spent, and she has already found her way around our file structure.

Nicole reports to Jennifer Vasquez, Consulting Actuary. Her work is data intake, file checks and first drafts of exhibits. Intake comes first in a valuation, and an error that gets past intake is carried into every number after it. So when a census or asset file arrives, Nicole will check it against the prior year and against what the client told us to expect. She will write down exactly what she found. What a finding means is for the reviewing actuary to decide. We keep those two steps apart on purpose, and our reports keep them apart as well. If a file is late, or arrives in a different layout from the one we received last year, she should tell the analyst on the engagement the same day, so that the schedule can be adjusted while there is still room to adjust it.

Our wording on data reliance and on the qualifications attached to a result has been worked out over many reports, and she should learn it before she writes any of it. Her first period covers the following:

items: 1. Read the standard reliance and qualification paragraphs, then read them in place in a recently issued valuation report.
2. Run the intake checklist on the next census file that arrives, alongside the analyst on that engagement.
3. Keep a log for each file she checks: what was received, what was tested, and what did not reconcile.
4. Draft one set of exhibits from a completed valuation and go through the draft line by line with the reviewer.
5. Meet with Jennifer Vasquez each week through the end of the summer, and less often once they agree the work needs less review.

blocks.text: There is no deadline on these items beyond doing them carefully and writing down what was done. Robert Lawrence will sit in on one of the weekly meetings once Nicole has had a couple of months with us, to hear how the work is going and what we should change for her. Questions are welcome at any stage of a check, and Jennifer Vasquez would prefer to hear them early.
